<!-- pr-reviewer: 0d6039f851496fda0919062ef3728d9cf5a7a9f5 -->
**Ready for the maintainer to merge.**

## What looks good
- The new code only runs after `ruststep::parser::parse` has already failed (`step.rs:48-55`), so no valid file's import result can change; the fallback keeps ruststep's own message when every record parses alone.
- No `unwrap`/`expect`/`panic!` and no unchecked indexing in `step_diag.rs`: the slices sit on ASCII boundaries (`;`, `/*`, `*/`), and `keyword_is` guards with `is_char_boundary`.
- Linear scan, one pass. Non-UTF8 is refused before it is reached (`step.rs:46`).
- Provenance line present, file is 177 lines, decision file included, no process files, deps, build.rs or snapshot PNGs touched.

## Local results (merged with upstream/main, clean merge)
| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo test -p camcraft-app --test import` (whole suite, includes the 3 new fns) | 26 passed |
| `--test step_chord_units` (gate-mapped) | 3 passed |
| `cargo clippy -p camcraft-app --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |

Extra malformed-input probes, run through `import::parse_model` with a throwaway test that is not part of the PR:
- empty, 5-byte, 50-byte and mid-file truncations, non-UTF8, and multibyte text (`Ä`, `é€😀`, inside strings, comments and bare records): all clean errors, no panic.
- a 20 MB single-line entity with a bad record: error in ~0.5 s, text truncated to 80 chars.
- 300k records followed by a bad `#999999`: reports `#999999` at line 300003 in ~0.35 s.
- a damaged id (`#9x =`) is still named as `entity #9` at line 16, which matches the fixture's real line.

## Requested before merge
None.

## Notes (not blocking)
1. A file truncated inside DATA after the last complete record, with no trailing `;`, falls back to ruststep's unchanged "Error while tokenizing STEP input ... at line 7: DATA;" message, so #887's complaint still applies to that shape. A follow-up could name the dangling final record.
2. `check_record` skips only leading comments, so a comment in the middle of a record is passed to `entity_instance`. I did not test this. It can only matter for the blame on a file that already failed.

A maintainer will approve and merge by hand.

<!-- pr-reviewer: 4f30294760ba6430c4bd33a1d28d1fc9e666d46d -->
**Independent review (high tier) - Ready for the maintainer to merge**

This review is by a reviewer that did not write the PR. The earlier comments on this head came from the author's own account.

**What looks good**
- It only changes the message. `step_diag::locate` runs only inside the `map_err` of a parse that has already failed (`step.rs:92-99`), so a file that failed before still fails, and a file that imported before takes exactly the same path. Nothing is skipped and no partial geometry is produced.
- The merge with main is clean. Against `origin/main`, `step.rs` differs only in that one `map_err` hunk, and `mod.rs` only adds `mod step_diag;`. The #911 reduced-fidelity flag and `step_refine::refine` are untouched.
- The scanner is a small framing pass, not a second STEP grammar. It splits records on `;` outside `'..'` strings (with `''` escapes) and `/* */` comments, and each record is judged by ruststep's own `entity_instance`. It is linear: each byte is visited once and each record is parsed once. A 14 MB / 300k-entity file with the bad entity last gave the right `#id` and line in 3.6 s in debug, and most of that is ruststep's own failed parse.
- Panic safety: every slice index sits on an ASCII byte (`;`, `/*`, `*/`, `#`) or follows a trim, and `keyword_is` checks `is_char_boundary`. There is no unwrap, expect or panic. Non-UTF-8 input is refused before this code runs.
- The fixture is our own `empty_list.step` with one comma removed (#9), and its origin is stated. The provenance line is present, `step_diag.rs` is 177 lines, the decision file and `Changelog:` line are there, and the message is plain English.

**Local results (trial-merged with main a6bd69d8, no conflicts, Windows, `core.autocrlf=true`)**
| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| `--test import` (incl. 3 new `step_parse_error_*`) | 26 passed |
| `--test step_chord_units` | 3 passed |
| `--test model_fidelity` | 9 passed |
| `--test step_fidelity` | 2 passed |
| `--test large_models` | 3 passed, 1 ignored (heavy lane) |
| `--test bore_facet_sagitta` | 2 passed |
| `--lib step` | 11 passed |
| `clippy -p camcraft-app --all-targets -D warnings` | clean |

**CRLF.** On this checkout the new fixture is CRLF, and the diagnostic still says `entity #9 at line 16`, which is correct. Lines are counted on `\n` in the bytes actually read, so LF and CRLF give the same number. I also ran a local throwaway probe (not committed) with these cases, and each got the right `#id` and line:
- the first entity bad (line 8) and the last entity bad (line 178), in both LF and CRLF;
- a record that spans several lines;
- a comment holding `;` and `'`, and strings holding `;` and `''`;
- `/**/`, `/*/ */` and `*/` inside a record;
- a complex entity `#7 = (A() B(,))`;
- a missing `;` before `ENDSEC`;
- multibyte characters (é) next to every slice point;
- unterminated strings and comments at end of file;
- a 26-digit `#id`;
- empty, `;;;;` and `DATA;#;` inputs.

An error in the HEADER section falls back to ruststep's own message, which is the intended behaviour.

**Requested before merge**
None.

**Notes (non-blocking)**
1. Deeply nested parentheses overflow the stack. This predates the PR: main does it too. A DATA record with about 1000 or more nested `(` (for example `#900 = A((((…;` inside an otherwise valid file) makes ruststep's recursive parser overflow the stack in debug. That aborts the process, and main fails at the same depth. The PR adds no new depth: `locate` runs the same parser on the same record, only after the full parse has already failed. It is worth a follow-up issue (cap the paren depth before `ruststep::parser::parse`, or parse on a thread with a large stack) under the Prime Directive "corrupt file -> clean error, not a crash". It is not this PR's defect.
2. `step_diag.rs:86` replaces `\n` with a space in the quoted record text, but a CRLF file leaves a stray `\r` in a multi-line record's snippet. `replace(['\r', '\n'], " ")` would fix that. It is cosmetic.
3. A file with old-Mac CR-only line ends reports `line 1` because only `\n` is counted. Such files are rare, and the `#id` is still right.
4. `DATAé;` (garbage glued to the keyword) reports "no DATA section found". That is acceptable; the file is refused either way.

A maintainer will approve and merge by hand.
